lesson.title: Barack Obama and a Nation in Crisis
lesson.summary: Barack Obama's election in November 2008 as the first Black president of the United States came amid economic collapse, and his presidency from 2009 to 2017 was defined by efforts to steer the country through recovery while pursuing major reforms at home and a shifting American role abroad.
lesson.body:
Barack Obama, a first term U.S. senator from Illinois, won the presidency in November 2008, defeating Republican nominee John McCain in an election dominated by the unfolding financial crisis. Inaugurated on January 20, 2009, Obama became the first African American president in the nation's history, a milestone that carried enormous symbolic weight against the backdrop of the country's long history of racial exclusion and struggle.

Obama's first priority was confronting the Great Recession he inherited. Within weeks of taking office, he signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a stimulus package worth roughly 800 billion dollars aimed at saving jobs and jump starting economic growth, and his administration extended emergency loans to rescue General Motors and Chrysler from collapse. In 2010 he signed the Dodd Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, a sweeping overhaul of financial regulation designed to prevent a repeat of the 2008 crisis by increasing oversight of banks and complex financial products.

Obama's most significant and controversial domestic achievement was the Affordable Care Act, signed in March 2010, though his presidency included other major shifts as well, including the 2010 and 2011 repeal of the Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy that had barred openly gay Americans from serving in the military. Abroad, Obama worked to wind down the wars he had inherited, withdrawing American combat troops from Iraq by the end of 2011 even as he temporarily surged troops into Afghanistan, and he authorized the raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Pakistan on May 2, 2011, nearly a decade after the September 11 attacks bin Laden had orchestrated.

Obama won reelection in 2012 over Republican challenger Mitt Romney, but his presidency also coincided with rising political polarization, including the emergence of the conservative Tea Party movement and repeated clashes with a Republican controlled Congress that produced government shutdowns and standoffs over the federal budget and debt ceiling. By the time he left office in January 2017, the economy had recovered from the crisis of 2008 and 2009, though slowly and unevenly, and his presidency had reshaped debates over health care, financial regulation, and America's role in the world that would continue to define American politics for years afterward.
